items.answer: An MIT online experiment (published in Nature, 2018) that collected about 40 million decisions on how autonomous vehicles should resolve dilemmas

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Most consumer cars with "self-driving" features still require constant driver supervision.
Reason (R): These systems are mainly SAE Level 2 driver assistance.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Level 2 needs a supervising human driver.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Self-driving cars are already programmed to choose whom to kill in a crash." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Developers focus on avoiding collisions and reducing speed; there is no evidence that deployed systems make explicit trolley-problem choices about victims.
items.markingKey: Developers focus on avoiding collisions and reducing speed; there is no evidence that deployed systems make explicit trolley-problem choices about victims. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"In the event of unavoidable accident situations, any distinction based on personal features (age, gender, physical or mental constitution) is strictly prohibited."
— German Ethics Commission on Automated and Connected Driving, Rule 9, 2017

With reference to the source, explain which ethical approach the rule reflects.
items.answer: A deontological, rights-based approach: every person has equal dignity, so the car must not weigh lives by personal characteristics, even if a utilitarian calculation might favour it.
items.markingKey: A deontological, rights-based approach: every person has equal dignity, so the car must not weigh lives by personal characteristics, even if a utilitarian calculation might favour it. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A robotaxi company reports 75 injury-causing crashes over 22 million driverless miles. A comparable human-driver benchmark in the same cities is 4.8 injury crashes per million miles. Calculate the robotaxi rate per million miles and the percentage difference from the human benchmark.
items.answer: 3.41 per million miles; 29% lower than human drivers

items.stem: With reference to the MIT Moral Machine experiment, explain how it illustrates values and ethics in AV design.
items.answer: Researchers collected about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories about whom an autonomous car should spare; preferences varied between cultural clusters. There is no universal moral code for machines, so programming ethical choices raises questions about whose values apply.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers collected about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories about whom an autonomous car should spare; preferences varied between cultural clusters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Evaluate who should be held responsible when an autonomous vehicle causes a fatal crash, using at least one real case.
items.answer: Tempe 2018 (Uber, safety driver), Cruise 2023, Tesla Autopilot cases; manufacturer vs software developer vs operator vs regulator; product liability; UK Automated Vehicles Act 2024 (authorised self-driving entity responsible); judgement.
items.markingKey: Tempe 2018 (Uber, safety driver), Cruise 2023, Tesla Autopilot cases; manufacturer vs software developer vs operator vs regulator; product liability; UK Automated Vehicles Act 2024 (authorised self-driving entity responsible); judgement.

items.stem: "Autonomous vehicles should be allowed on public roads only if they are proven safer than human drivers." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: AVs should be allowed in limited domains with strong safety data and independent oversight, expanding as evidence accumulates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: protects the public from unproven technology; human drivers cause most crashes, so the bar is meaningful. items.stem: Explain why the trolley problem is criticised as a guide for autonomous-vehicle ethics.
items.answer: Real crashes rarely involve clear choices between known victims; engineers focus on avoiding crashes, sensors give uncertain information, and the bigger ethical questions are about safety standards, testing, liability and who bears risk.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Tempe crash raised questions about responsibility.
items.answer: The car's system failed to classify the pedestrian correctly, Uber had disabled automatic emergency braking, and the safety driver was distracted; responsibility was spread between company, software and operator, and only the driver was prosecuted.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a utilitarian approach to AV dilemmas and a deontological approach to AV dilemmas.
items.answer: A utilitarian approach programs cars to minimise total harm (e.g. fewer deaths); a deontological approach sets rules that must not be broken (e.g. never deliberately target a person, or not discriminate by age), regardless of outcomes.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Lethal autonomous weapons should be banned by an international treaty."
items.answer: A treaty prohibiting weapons without meaningful human control and regulating others is ethically justified, though achieving it is politically difficult.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "trolley problem"?
options: The amount of output produced per unit of input, such as per worker-hour
An MIT online experiment (published in Nature, 2018) that collected about 40 million decisions on how autonomous vehicles should resolve dilemmas
A thought experiment (Philippa Foot, 1967) about whether to divert a runaway trolley to kill one person instead of five, used to discuss dilemmas for autonomous vehicles
Respect for a person's worth, autonomy and privacy, which care technologies should protect
items.answer: A thought experiment (Philippa Foot, 1967) about whether to divert a runaway trolley to kill one person instead of five, used to discuss dilemmas for autonomous vehicles
items.markingKey: C. "trolley problem" is a thought experiment (Philippa Foot, 1967) about whether to divert a runaway trolley to kill one person instead of five, used to discuss dilemmas for autonomous vehicles.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "robot-assisted surgery"?
options: Surgery in which a surgeon controls robotic instruments, often for minimally invasive procedures
A society in which the proportion of older people is growing, increasing demand for care
The amount of output produced per unit of input, such as per worker-hour
The energy used to make a product, such as the materials and manufacturing of a robot
items.answer: Surgery in which a surgeon controls robotic instruments, often for minimally invasive procedures
items.markingKey: A. "robot-assisted surgery" is surgery in which a surgeon controls robotic instruments, often for minimally invasive procedures.

items.stem: Which of these is an environmental benefit of agricultural robots?
items.answer: Targeted spraying that reduces pesticide use
items.markingKey: Targeted spraying that reduces pesticide use. Weeding robots and smart sprayers can cut chemical use.

items.stem: Distinguish between an autonomous weapon and an automated weapon.
items.answer: An automated weapon follows fixed pre-set rules (e.g. a mine or a missile-defence system reacting to incoming projectiles); an autonomous weapon selects and engages targets in changing environments without human decision for each attack.
items.markingKey: An automated weapon follows fixed pre-set rules (e.g. a mine or a missile-defence system reacting to incoming projectiles); an autonomous weapon selects and engages targets in changing environments without human decision for each attack. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why robot-assisted surgery is not always better than conventional surgery.
items.answer: It is expensive, requires specialist training, and for many procedures studies show similar outcomes to conventional laparoscopic surgery; benefits depend on the procedure and surgeon experience.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is expensive, requires specialist training, and for many procedures studies show similar outcomes to conventional laparoscopic surgery; benefits depend on the procedure and surgeon experience. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between job creation from automation and job displacement.
items.answer: Displacement is the loss of jobs when tasks are automated (e.g. assembly-line roles); creation includes new jobs in designing, installing, maintaining and programming robots and in growing firms.
items.markingKey: Displacement is the loss of jobs when tasks are automated (e.g. assembly-line roles); creation includes new jobs in designing, installing, maintaining and programming robots and in growing firms. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): An international treaty currently bans all lethal autonomous weapons.
Reason (R): States have discussed lethal autonomous weapons under the CCW in Geneva.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. There is no specific ban treaty yet; R is true.

items.stem: "Robotic surgery has no risks because machines do not make mistakes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Robotic surgery can have malfunctions and surgical errors, and lawsuits and FDA reports have documented injuries; the surgeon remains responsible.
items.markingKey: Robotic surgery can have malfunctions and surgical errors, and lawsuits and FDA reports have documented injuries; the surgeon remains responsible. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why automation can increase productivity but also inequality.
items.answer: Robots produce more output per worker-hour and lower costs, but the gains may go mainly to owners and highly skilled workers while displaced routine workers lose jobs or bargaining power.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Robots produce more output per worker-hour and lower costs, but the gains may go mainly to owners and highly skilled workers while displaced routine workers lose jobs or bargaining power. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A robotaxi company reports 31 injury-causing crashes over 22 million driverless miles. A comparable human-driver benchmark in the same cities is 3.2 injury crashes per million miles. Calculate the robotaxi rate per million miles and the percentage difference from the human benchmark.
items.answer: 1.41 per million miles; 56% lower than human drivers

items.stem: Using the da Vinci Surgical System as an example, explain robot-assisted surgery.
items.answer: Millions of procedures have been performed with da Vinci systems worldwide; studies show benefits for some procedures (e.g. prostatectomy blood loss) but high costs. Precision tools enhance surgeons' abilities, but costs and uneven evidence raise questions of value and equitable access.
items.markingKey: Context (Millions of procedures have been performed with da Vinci systems worldwide; studies show benefits for some procedures (e.g. prostatectomy blood loss) but high costs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe Acemoglu and Restrepo's study of US robots and explain what it reveals about automation and inequality.
items.answer: Their research on US labour markets (1990–2007) found that areas more exposed to industrial robots saw lower employment and wages. The evidence shows that robot gains were not automatically shared with workers in exposed communities.
items.markingKey: Context (Their research on US labour markets (1990–2007) found that areas more exposed to industrial robots saw lower employment and wages.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the evidence shows that robot gains were not automatically shared with workers in exposed communities. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to automation and inequality.

items.stem: A student claims: "Self-driving cars are already programmed to choose whom to kill in a crash." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Developers focus on avoiding collisions and reducing speed; there is no evidence that deployed systems make explicit trolley-problem choices about victims.
items.markingKey: Developers focus on avoiding collisions and reducing speed; there is no evidence that deployed systems make explicit trolley-problem choices about victims. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe care robots in Japan and explain what it reveals about robots in care.
items.answer: Japan has funded robots such as Paro, the lifting robot ROBEAR and the communication robot Pepper in care homes; a 2023 study found uptake limited because robots often added work for staff. Care robots offer support in an ageing society, but practical problems and the value of human care limit their impact.
items.markingKey: Context (Japan has funded robots such as Paro, the lifting robot ROBEAR and the communication robot Pepper in care homes; a 2023 study found uptake limited because robots often added work for staff.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Right now, the human worker who does, say, $50,000 worth of work in a factory, that income is taxed. If a robot comes in to do the same thing, you'd think that we'd tax the robot at a similar level."
— Bill Gates, interview with Quartz, 2017

With reference to the source, explain the argument for a robot tax.
items.answer: When robots replace workers, governments lose income tax revenue; taxing robots would maintain revenue to fund retraining and social support, and might slow displacement.
items.markingKey: When robots replace workers, governments lose income tax revenue; taxing robots would maintain revenue to fund retraining and social support, and might slow displacement. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using the MIT Moral Machine experiment as an example, explain values and ethics in AV design.
items.answer: Researchers collected about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories about whom an autonomous car should spare; preferences varied between cultural clusters. There is no universal moral code for machines, so programming ethical choices raises questions about whose values apply.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers collected about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories about whom an autonomous car should spare; preferences varied between cultural clusters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: there is no universal moral code for machines, so programming ethical choices raises questions about whose values apply. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to values and ethics in AV design.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The benefits of robot-assisted surgery justify its costs."
items.answer: It is justified for procedures where evidence shows clear benefits, but not as a universal replacement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precision, smaller incisions and faster recovery for some procedures; ergonomics for surgeons. Arguments against: high purchase and maintenance costs; similar outcomes to laparoscopic surgery for many procedures; may widen inequality between hospitals. Supported judgement: It is justified for procedures where evidence shows clear benefits, but not as a universal replacement.

items.stem: "Robotics will help more than harm environmental sustainability." Discuss.
items.answer: Robotics can support sustainability in targeted uses if powered by clean energy and designed for repair and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precision agriculture reduces chemicals and water; efficient manufacturing and recycling robots (sorting e-waste). Arguments against: production uses energy, metals and rare minerals; more automation may increase consumption; e-waste at end of life. Supported judgement: Robotics can support sustainability in targeted uses if powered by clean energy and designed for repair and recycling. items.stem: "Lethal autonomous weapons should be banned by an international treaty." Discuss.
items.answer: A treaty prohibiting weapons without meaningful human control and regulating others is ethically justified, though achieving it is politically difficult.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: responsibility gap and lack of human judgement; risk of arms races and proliferation; UN Secretary-General and many states support limits.
